title: The black stone lifted together
hook: at thirty-five he settles the tribes' quarrel over the stone with a cloak (sirah)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ali, who in a hard year, Abu Talib's son came to live with the Prophet and Khadijah. Your line was: raised in that house. Whose load did you lighten? Day seven hundred twenty-one.

Before the quarrel, there was a rule about money. The Ka'ba was old and damaged, and the clans of Quraysh agreed to pull it down and build it again. Ibn Ishaq says one of their elders stood up and told them: put nothing into this House but clean money. Nothing earned from usury, nothing from prostitution, nothing taken unjustly from anyone. They agreed. So they gathered only clean money, and built, clan by clan, wall by wall. Today: al-Amin.
screen: `AN OLD HOUSE, DAMAGED.` → `ONLY CLEAN MONEY.` → `CLAN BY CLAN, WALL BY WALL.`

segments.voice: Clean money ran short. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, from 'Aishah, says the Prophet told her that her people's funds fell short, and so a part of the old House was left outside the new walls. That's the space behind the low curved wall on one side of the Ka'ba, the Hijr. Pilgrims circle outside it, because it belongs to the House. The Qur'an remembers who raised the House's foundations. Pickthall's words: "And when Abraham and Ishmael were raising the foundations of the House." So the clans of Mecca were rebuilding, imperfectly, something they believed Ibrahim had begun. Then came the corner where the Black Stone sits, and every clan wanted the honor of setting it in place. Ibn Ishaq says the quarrel went on for days, and the clans came close to fighting. They agreed to let the next man through the gate decide. It was the one they called al-Amin, the trustworthy; Ibn Ishaq says he was thirty-five. He asked for a cloak, laid the stone on it, and had a man from each clan take hold of the edge. They lifted it together, and he set it in the wall with his own hand. This closes a week of the household. The trustworthy one. Khadijah's caravan. Her proposal. Their children, every one remembered. Zayd, who chose to stay. Ali, raised in that house. And a cloak with room for every hand. Next comes the mountain, and the revelation.
screen: `CLEAN MONEY RAN SHORT.` · `THE HIJR, LEFT OUTSIDE.` · `A STONE ON A CLOAK.` · `A WEEK IN THE HOUSEHOLD.` · then, large: `EVERYONE A CORNER.`

segments.voice: The practice: solve a quarrel so everyone shares. Settle, and breathe. Think of a disagreement near you, at work, at home, in a group chat, where each side wants the honor or the last word. Don't pick a winner. Picture the cloak instead. What would let every person take hold of an edge? A shared task. A decision made together. Credit spread around. Let one idea come, small and practical. If you pray, you can ask for wisdom in it. The bell holds the time.
Al-Amin, the trustworthy. The name Quraysh called him when the clans feared fighting over the Black Stone, and he set it in place so every clan could lift it together. Today's word.
Your line: everyone a corner. Today, in one shared task, make sure every person has a real piece of it, and say whose hands were on it. Day seven hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Pilgrims circling the Ka'ba pass outside the curved wall of the Hijr, and touch, kiss or gesture toward the Black Stone, following the Prophet's ﷺ example.

trapdoor: what you thought: a clever trick to stop a fight.
what it means: a rebuilding done with clean money only, finished by a man who gave every clan a share of the honor.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari's hadith of 'Aishah explains the Hijr; Ibn Ishaq gives the clean-money rule and the cloak.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1584 (the Hijr: 'your people's funds fell short')
Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (rebuilding the Ka'ba; clean money only; the quarrel; the cloak; his age thirty-five)

notes: Ibn Ishaq names the elder as Abu Wahb ibn 'Amr (al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah begins the demolition); left unnamed here. Confirm the clean-money paraphrase.
'The quarrel went on for days' (Ibn Ishaq: four or five nights) and 'swords nearly came out' (the bowl of blood) paraphrased; confirm.
Age thirty-five attributed to Ibn Ishaq as the index requires; confirm it is his figure.
Sahih al-Bukhari 1584: confirm number and that the hadith's wording supports 'funds fell short'.
Pickthall 2:127 opening quoted from memory; confirm wording.
Week-end look back (days 715–721) and pointer to the revelation part (722–731). Year 1 day 84 told the cloak story; this day leads with the clean-money rule and the Hijr to avoid repeating it.

Editor: 'who laid the first foundations' changed to 'who raised the House's foundations' (2:127 does not say 'first'); 'pilgrims still walk around it' to 'pilgrims circle outside it'; 'swords nearly came out' to 'the clans came close to fighting' (closer to Ibn Ishaq's bowl-of-blood oath).

Audit: the Hijr is the enclosed space the curved wall marks, not the wall itself (Bukhari 1584 asks about the area left out); wording fixed. Myth 'he set the stone in place by himself' was false-marked though the script says he set it with his own hand; replaced with 'one clan won the honor of lifting the stone' (false).
